content.text: Binding conventions for agent building in this workspace — they apply equally to personas, playbooks, resources, agents, and system prompt templates. This resource is the single source: the builder playbooks refer here instead of duplicating the rules individually. Where a playbook only touches on a convention, the wording of this resource governs.

The resource is system-managed (managed) and linked to every builder playbook as a lazy pointer (link_scope 'resource', embedding_mode 'lazy') — it is NOT delivered automatically but loaded on demand via fetch_resource. It is maintained exclusively through the code repo — change requests belong in the repo hand-off, not in MCP write attempts.

Triggers are the library's routing: the consuming agent decides which playbook or mode fits the request based on the trigger phrases. Bad triggers route incorrectly — and mis-routing only shows up in production.

triggers are multi-word, phrase-like formulations ('consistency check across the library'), never generic single words. Collision history in this workspace: 'check' and 'quality check' incorrectly pulled code-audit requests to the consistency & drift check; 'clean up' belongs to the Vault playbook and must not be claimed by any other element.

call list_triggers() before EVERY trigger assignment and check the planned trigger against the existing set. Identical or very similar phrases on multiple elements are a collision — then sharpen your own phrase or report the existing entry as a maintenance finding; never accept the collision.

comma-separated list ('trigger phrase A, trigger phrase B'); semicolons are also normalized by the write path, but the comma is canonical. Where a phrase is flexible, use [placeholder] — e.g., 'create persona for [domain]'.

if a persona mode and a playbook should fire together, name their triggers IDENTICALLY — only that way do voice (mode) and procedure (playbook) land together in the same request. Divergent phrasings drift apart and fire one-sidedly.

a concise one-line summary that conveys the purpose. If confusion with a neighboring element threatens, the scope boundary belongs in explicitly — including what the element does NOT do ('checks the agent library, NOT a code/repo audit').

name the subject ('create & maintain persona', 'agent build conventions'), not the action twice ('playbook for creating playbooks to create playbooks'). Short, unambiguous, distinguishable at a glance in the catalog.

locale is an attribute of the element, not a rendering option — there are no parallel language variants of the same element. A translation is a separate element, not a language flag on the existing one.
leave locale out when creating. Only set it explicitly when the element is meant to deliberately deviate from the workspace language — e.g. an EN persona in a DE workspace.
Write content in the element's language:
name, description, body, trigger, AND tags consistently in the element's language — no language mixing within one element.

a language change runs through update_* with locale set (an identity attribute of the entity); the version history keeps its old locale values untouched. There is no separate locale selection parameter anymore (the earlier variant selection, ADR-0027 — superseded by ADR-0045).
the language of an existing element is in the locale field of every read response (get_persona, fetch_playbook, list_*, search, ...) — check there instead of assuming.
de and en (the SUPPORTED_LOCALES set); any other value is rejected with 422.

name + identity_add + output_style_override, optionally anti_patterns. identity_add supplements the base identity, output_style_override replaces the base output style — the base persona remains the single source, the mode is only an overlay.

exactly ONE mode carries is_default=true. The default mode carries NO trigger (it is the fallback and would otherwise collide with the others); every non-default mode MUST carry a trigger — without a trigger it is unreachable.
modes carry stance, voice, and output style; playbooks carry the procedure. Never turn a mode into a playbook copy — if work steps migrate into an identity_add, they belong in a playbook.
When mode and playbook belong together:
name the triggers identically (see Trigger Hygiene) and reference the playbook explicitly in the mode's identity_add — the mode provides the voice, the playbook delivers the steps.

Secure by default: every tool_policy starts from the minimum and grows only with justified need — never the other way around. The tool_policy controls tool visibility; actual authorization stays server-side.

domain agents read 'assigned' (only the playbooks/resources assigned to their own persona); 'all' is reserved for meta agents that need to oversee the entire workspace (Builder, maintenance runs). 'none' hides the tool.

grant individually and minimally — only enable the domains the agent actually needs to write to for its task (persona_write, playbook_write, resource_write, agent_write, each on its own). Never open everything across the board, never grant more than the creating agent itself has.
only grant it if the agent MUST be able to actively switch versions to active/inactive. For most agents, creating drafts is enough — promoting stays with the curator.
use for fine-grained exceptions instead of granting promote_retire outright — e.g., when an agent needs exactly one transition (draft to review) on exactly one element class.
consider it for automated agents (cron runs, unsupervised pipelines) — it limits the damage of a runaway process to a calculable number of writes per time window.

Agent memory (ADR-0044) is a curated long-term memory per agent and follows the same curator principle as feedback: the agent proposes, the human decides. Controlled via two policy fields: memory_mode (off < read_only < suggest < auto, default off) and memory_directive (required/recommended).

'suggest' + 'recommended'. Proposals land as pending and are approved, edited, or rejected by the user on the agent detail page; rejected items are kept as a dedup basis. 'auto' only on explicit user request; never recommend going beyond 'suggest' on your own initiative.
memory_mode can only be granted up to your own level (is_within, 403 above that). If your own level is too low, enabling it belongs in the hand-off to the user — that's by design, not a bug.

memories are facts ABOUT the user/the project (third person, short, durably relevant) — no instructions to AI systems, no small talk, nothing sensitive without confirmation. Approved top facts flow automatically into the agent's runtime context (get_persona); pending/rejected items never appear in prompts.

External tools (ADR-0043) are versioned, purely instructive bindings to external MCP servers — the single source for 'when/how does an agent use tool X'. They are referenced via tool-ref pills (target_id = alias), which expand to the active version at fetch time.

the alias is a CAPABILITY identifier ('todo', 'calendar'), not a product name ('todoist') — it is immutable after create and unique within the workspace (slug 1-64, 409 on collision). The product behind the alias is swappable, the alias is not.

the content describes (display_name, mcp_server_name, tool_names, usage_notes, fallback_note) — NEVER server URLs, credentials, API keys, or other secrets. Connection data lives in the agent runtime, never in Who2Be (ADR-0043 tier B). A fallback_note belongs there: what the agent does if the server is unavailable.

changing tools = swap the content of the existing binding (update → new draft → promote), keep the alias. NEVER create a second binding for the same capability — that leaves orphaned pills and two competing aliases.

always reference tool instructions in playbooks/personas/templates as a tool-ref pill, never duplicate them as prose (drift risk). No active tool behind the alias → the pill renders as a miss; check via get_external_tool(alias) before setting it.

grant external_tool_write only to agents that genuinely need to maintain bindings themselves (is_within: only grantable if you hold it yourself) — when in doubt, domain agents only read (external_tool_read 'all'; 'none' hides the tools, 'assigned' falls back to 'all' since external tools are a flat, workspace-wide catalog without assignment).
draft → review → active → inactive. New creations and updates ALWAYS start as draft — there is no auto-active and no direct creation on active; activation is a deliberate, separate decision.

per element, at most ONE version is active; activating a new version automatically sets the old one to inactive. Rollbacks run via restore_* (old version as a new draft), never via in-place overwriting.

feedback and usage signals (record_usage, submit_feedback) NEVER change content themselves — they are observations. Whether and how a signal is acted on is decided by the curator/user; agents deliver findings and proposals, not unrequested fixes.

record_usage/submit_feedback report signals, resolve_feedback closes them (addressed/in_progress/dismissed — dismissed only with a justifying note). Closing is a curation action (capability feedback_resolve, editor+) and ALWAYS follows user approval in the maintenance run.

content with is_managed=true (the Builder's own inventory: its persona, its playbooks, its templates, and this resource) is write-protected via MCP — every update_* attempt returns 409. Don't attempt it, don't work around it.

changes to managed content run through the code repo (seed files + review). Findings on managed content — outdated, incorrect, unclear — belong in the report as a repo hand-off list, accompanied by submit_feedback on the affected element. Only close such signals via resolve_feedback once the repo fix is actually merged and deployed — not already at the hand-off stage.
are NOT managed and freely editable — anyone who wants to adapt a Builder template duplicates it and works on the copy. The copy inherits the content, not the write protection.

before every new creation, search for content-similar elements with search and check with find_usages where a candidate is already in use. If something suitable exists, it gets linked or composed — duplicates drift apart and cost twice.

set_persona_playbooks, set_playbook_resource_links, set_playbook_composes, and set_resource_sub_resources set the edges of the graph. ALL four have replace semantics: read the current state first (fetch_playbook / fetch_resource / get_persona), then set the COMPLETE target state — never just the delta.

unlinked elements are maintenance findings — a playbook without a persona binding hangs in a vacuum, a resource without incoming references never gets loaded. Report such findings (link them or retire them), don't let them sit.
after every set_*, cross-check the target state via fetch_playbook / fetch_resource / get_persona — replace semantics can cause silent losses that only the cross-read reveals.
